posts.name: FrivYeti
posts.cooked:
Trajector:

FRG owned a few other gaming imprints. Do we know what happened to those? Are they pulling back from everything tabletop, or just GTG?

It certainly looks like everything tabletop.

Flat River games sold Synapses Games and Luma Imports to ACD Distribution (and then sold Compile, Get Bit, and Medium to Synapse Games), which included having three employees that I think they hired as part of acquiring Luma leave to reform it under ACD. They also returned Cheapass Games to Crab Fragment Labs, so that’s out.

With those groups gone, I’m pretty sure that Greater Than Games is their only tabletop subsidiary. I went to see if there were any games under distribution that weren’t covered by the sales aside from Sentinels and Spirit Island, but the Greater than Games store page is still advertising Synapse and Cheapass games (presumably they have deal to sell off warehouse stock?) so the following information might be wrong.

In addition to GtG, Synapse, and Cheapass, the GtG webstore seems to have games from a variety of European publishers. I think those publishers are all under the Luma license, but I’m not actually sure. They’ve also got a handful of games from Darrington Press, but not their newer games, and a handful of distribution of American miniature games, which I have no idea if they’re still doing or not.

Rabit:

Wow. I imagine there were a lot of people complaining about paying for a thing multiple times.

That wasn’t quite what happened. The guy/small business that created the original project overpromised on stretch goals, couldn’t handle them all, and wound up having a heart attacke that closed his business and saw him leave gaming altogether. A friend of his with a similar business agreed to step in and try to fulfill the project (in exchange for the rights to the figures and molds that had been done, which he hoped to sell at retail after the KS was finished. That led to partial fulfillment, but he overreached as well and wound having to admit he’d never finish everything, so another guy came along, picked up the rights, and did his best to continue fulfillment. That was the stage where i got everything I’d backed for, plus another pledge that someone sold me, plus some extras that I agreed to pay for to help Guy #3 pay postage on my stuff and some other pledges (by that point I figured we’d never see retail sales, so I wanted everything I’d ever need while I could get it). I only got everything because I was a merciless pest about it to three different people, and because i was willing to throw some actual outside-of-KS-funds money to speed the process up. I think there may be a fourth business involved now but I haven’t really paid attention. Last I was involved about 2/3rds of the backers had their stuff, and AFAIK none of them paid multiple times for their pledges - but I know a few did what i did and agreed to order some extra figs at retail to keep the engine sputtering along.

Convoluted as it sounds, it actually wasn’t the worst kickfailure I’ve been involved with, but it was the last of them. No more crowdfunding for me, no matter what.

Still haven’t painted all of the minis, but the ones I have finished are pretty neat, so there’s that, anyway.

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
That’s actually a really good story, to be honest.

I understand being done with crowdfunding. It’s infuriating how things can go, sometimes. I’ve been trying hard to limit myself. I actually have quite a few that are years old, at this point, but are still updating / being worked on. (I … made some poor choices during the early pandemic times… )

posts.name: Chief Lackey Rich
posts.cooked:
Given the number of actual, truly malicious kickscammers out there (many of them serial fraudsters with multiple fake projects they owe for) it’s actually kind of nice to see how often someone with zero responsibility to do so will step up and try to finish fulfillment when a creator blows it for one reason or another. Sometimes they’re backers themselves who are determined to get their stuff or die trying, sometime they’re folks in the same industry/hobby niche who can afford to make things better and maybe hope to take over the ready-made audience for future sales someday, and sometimes they just feel bad for the backers and the creator and enjoy playing fulfillment angel for both of them.

Sadly, I think you have to get really lucky for something like that to happen. Usually a kickfail is just a kickfail and ends badly for most or all of the people who backed.
